props.title: I Was Born, But...

sections.content: Yasujirō Ozu's **I Was Born, But...** (1932) stands as one of silent cinema's most penetrating examinations of childhood disillusionment and social hierarchy. The film follows two young brothers who discover their father's subordinate position at work, shattering their idealized view of him as a figure of authority. This masterwork influenced later coming-of-age films like **400 Blows** (1959) and **Yi Yi** (2000), particularly in their unflinching portrayal of children confronting adult realities. Ozu's signature low-angle shots and careful composition create an intimate perspective that puts us at child-height, experiencing their world directly.

sections.content: The film's exploration of social class through children's eyes resonates with later Japanese classics like **Grave of the Fireflies** (1988) and Nobody Knows (2004). Ozu's technique of letting scenes play out in long, static shots influenced an entire generation of Asian filmmakers, particularly Edward Yang and Hirokazu Kore-eda. The comedy emerges naturally from childhood behavior while never undermining the serious themes about social status and parental authority.

Ozu's mastery of silent film grammar makes **I Was Born, But...** (1932) particularly significant as one of his last silent works before transitioning to sound. His careful pacing and visual storytelling would carry through to later masterpieces like Tokyo Story (1953) and **Late Spring** (1949). The film's influence extends beyond Japan, visible in works like **The White Balloon** (1995) and **The 400 Blows** (1959), which similarly capture childhood's complex emotional landscape. sections.content: The revolutionary aspect of **I Was Born, But...** (1932) lies in its refusal to sentimentalize childhood. Unlike Hollywood contemporaries like **Little Rascals** shorts or later works such as **Stand By Me** (1986), Ozu presents children as complex social beings navigating power structures. This approach influenced neorealist works like **Germany Year Zero** (1948) and contemporary films such as **Petite Maman** (2021), which similarly respect children's capacity to grapple with difficult realities.
